newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's search for Albright ended in kitchen.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's search for Albright ended in kitchen.

text.p: The search for President Bill Clinton's new secretary of state began about a month before he won re-election and ended late on Wednesday night in the White House kitchen.

White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta, speaking shortly after Clinton named Madeleine Albright as his new secretary of state on Thursday, said he learned of the decision when he was summoned in the middle of a dance with his wife at the White House to meet Clinton in his private kitchen.

Along with Albright's appointment, Clinton named retiring Republican Sen. William Cohen as secretary of defence, Anthony Lake as director of the Central Intelligence Agency and Samuel Berger as national security adviser.
"The final decison was not made until last night and it came during the Congressional Ball, at which time I was having a dance with my wife," Panetta told reporters.

"We sat down in the kitchen upstairs, and he basically said I think I've come to a conclusion here, that I'd like to have Madeleine Albright as secretary of state and Bill Cohen as secretary of defence," he added.

Seeking to blunt criticism that Clinton has dithered over the appointments, the White House on Thursday produced its two top staff officials -- outgoing chief of staff Panetta and his incoming replacement Erskine Bowles -- to explain how Clinton made up his mind.
Bowles, a North Carolina banker with a carefully composed manner, argued that Clinton made the decision in an orderly fashion, adding the White House was ahead of its internal schedule.

"We have had a process that has been I think fairly well organised from the beginning," he said. "We have moved forward against some very firm timelines, we are ahead of those timelines and ahead of where we had wanted to be."

Bowles said the White House had aimed to make its decision on the appointments by the end of the year and to send them to Congress in the first week of January. He said it hoped to have some officials confirmed by the Jan. 20 inauguration.

Panetta said the White House began work on the transition three to four weeks before the Nov. 5 election, with four people leading the effort -- himself, Bowles, Washington lawyer Vernon Jordan and Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor.
Panetta said he canvassed members of the Cabinet to see who planned to retire if Clinton won a second term, and then began to come up with the names of possible replacements.
There was only one formal meeting with the president about the subject before the election, Panetta said, adding that the names of both Albright and Cohen came up at the time.
"We discussed the possibility of Madeleine Albright as secretary of state and Bill Cohen as defence secretary," he said. "We had thought very early on of the combination."

The White House may have generated some of the criticism about the time it has taken by telling reporters soon after the election that the president might name a new secretary of state before leaving for an Asia-Pacific trip on Nov. 15.
In a typical example, long-time Washington Post columnist Mary McGrory wrote on Thursday that: "The president is dithering over personnel choices he has known for months he would have to make."

The day Clinton returned from Asia on Nov. 27, Bowles handed him a fat binder outlining Cabinet options which he took the same day to the Camp David presidential retreat in Maryland, where he spent the long Thanksgiving weekend.

After a string of meetings and phone calls to seek views on the candidates, Clinton repaired to the golf course a week later and pondered the matter, returning in the evening to call Panetta to the kitchen and tell him he had made up his mind.
